title: Two Years Since the End of the Pandemic, Cannabis Continues Replacing Alcohol Socially

content_html_sanitized:
On May 5, 2023, two years ago this month, the World Health Organization declared that the COVID pandemic was officially over. See Timeline of the COVID-19 pandemic

Of course, that didn’t mean that no one was going to get sick and die, but people could start going out again and socializing with their friends.

The pandemic produced a number of changes that we hope will last. An online Harris Poll found that 45% of cannabis consumers aged 21 and up had replaced or reduced their alcohol consumption with marijuana since the beginning of the pandemic, and one-third of those who use cannabis recreationally prefer cannabis to drinking alcohol.

 Half of the respondents said they increased their cannabis use because cannabis helped them relax, and 48% said they did so to help them sleep. Of those who said they use marijuana recreationally, a third said that they prefer cannabis over alcohol. Interestingly, parents were actually turning to cannabis at higher rates than those without children. Think of the children! Another poll found that a majority plan to replace alcohol with cannabis.

See Big new study tracks cannabis replacing alcohol as a daily substance

And Marijuana replacing alcohol

And What happens when Alcohol is replaced by Cannabis?

And Now more Americans use cannabis daily than use alcohol daily.

The trend definitely continued, but with the pandemic over and people wanting to go out again, they were all dressed up, but had no place to go to use cannabis socially.

See Marijuana Social Clubs Are The Last Major Step for Legalization

Unfortunately, there are still not a lot of social venues where people can go and enjoy cannabis with their friends, so there is a real need for “Cannabis Social Clubs”, by whatever name.

The term actually started several years ago in Barcelona and spread to the rest of Spain, but the Spanish government has not been friendly, harassing the owners. Even in Barcelona, the clubs became victims of the backlash against “over tourism”.

See Will The Crackdown on Barcelona Cannabis Social Clubs Force the Legalization Issue in Spain?Unfortunately, no.

Germany to the rescue.  When Germany legalized recreational cannabis last year, they chose the term “Cannabis Social Club” for what is theoretically a grower’s cooperative. I think it is an overly complicated way of organizing, but it is a start.

Meanwhile in Las Vegas, one of the city’s two “Cannabis Consumption Lounges” closed it’s doors complaining about over regulation. There are lots of places to buy weed, but almost no place to smoke it. The casinos are afraid to allow cannabis consumption on their premises because of the risk of losing their enormously valuable gambling licenses until Federal laws or Schedules change. When that happens, they will all have cannabis lounges.

Meanwhile, back in California where it all started, the state passed a law legalizing “consumption lounges.” See Cannabis Consumption Lounges in California

On the other side of the country, New York made a mess of legalization, by delaying the permitting process for the 190 licensed cannabis dispensaries for New York City, population approximately 8 million. (Amsterdam has a population of a little less than 1 million, and 160 cannabis “coffee shops”,)

Surprisingly, the Prohibitionist New York Post carried an excellent article about the bureaucratic delays in approving places to smoke.

See NY cannabis merchants fume they can’t open pot lounges because of foot-dragging by regulators.

Finally, there is one more type of cannabis social club”, the originals created for patients at the beginning of the medical marijuana movement.

From 1997, see Calif. Court Rules Marijuana Clubs Illegal

We have come a long way since then, and patients in most states no longer live in fear of losing access to their medicine, but they still need a place to socialize. I will never forget visiting Dennis Peron’s club in San Francisco, and seeing how important it was for people who didn’t have much longer to live, being able to smoke a bit of weed with other patients and not be alone.
